Study 01 · Woodland Hills Topanga Willows: shade for a block that faces the afternoon sun A strip center with its storefronts facing west and a parking lot with one tree in it. Seven moves that keep the lot working and put most of it in shade. 17 new trees on the property 68 → 61 parking stalls 31 linked sources Read the study → Study 02 [NEXT SITE: a school quad or campus edge with no shade] Planned Study 03 [NEXT SITE: a stretch of street or a bus stop] Planned Method Four steps, in this order The order matters. The drawing comes second, and the proposal comes last. 1 Read the site Walk it, photograph it at the hottest hour, and draw what is really there in plan: the building, the stalls, the driveways, the trees. 2 Find the evidence Measured results only: government data, peer-reviewed studies and the city’s own code. Anything I cannot verify gets flagged. 3 Draw the fix A plan, a section and a detail that fit the site as it is. Then count what it costs, like parking stalls given up. 4 Say what is unknown Every study ends with its limits and with the numbers I would measure before and after to know whether it worked. Notes From the notebook Short pieces on what each study taught me. More as the studies come. The first plan I had for Topanga Willows was wrong. It showed the building at the back of the lot with parking in front, because that is what a strip center usually looks like. The aerial photo says otherwise. The building sits right on the sidewalk and all the parking is behind it. That one fact changed the whole argument: the storefronts face west into the afternoon sun, and the building only shades the first row of cars. Draw what is there before you draw what you want. The site had the answer. More notes → About I care about what happens between buildings I am Nathan, a student in the west San Fernando Valley, headed toward construction management. Redrawn Valley is where I practice the whole job on real places: reading a site, checking the rules, drawing the fix and being honest about the cost. pages.x: Topanga Willows | Redrawn Valley Case study Woodland Hills, Los Angeles Topanga Willows: shade for a block that faces the afternoon sun How one small shopping center on Topanga Canyon Boulevard, between Providencia Street and Dumetz Road, could get cooler, greener and worth staying at, using trees, soil and rain. Site Topanga Willows, 4900 Topanga Canyon Blvd [1] Type Retail strip center, about 9,800 sq ft [1] Focus Heat, shade, stormwater, places to sit Status Concept study. Not commissioned by the owner. By Nathan [Last name] Date [DATE] Fig. 1: the Topanga Canyon sidewalk, looking north. Showing: Proposed Concept sketch, not a rendering Today A west-facing walk with almost no shade One small street tree for a block-long row of storefronts. After noon the sun is on the paving and the glass. Proposed The same walk under a row of canopy Street trees fill the gaps, the lawn strip becomes native planting, and the storefronts get planters and a bench. Keep scrolling: the sketch has already changed. What is real here The research, the code requirements, and the layout of the site: where the building sits, the four rows of angled parking, the two driveways and the street trees are drawn from aerial imagery. [31] What is estimated Every dimension. I scaled them off the aerial, so expect them to be off by ten percent or so. The stall count (about 68), which shop is which at the south end, and where the existing seating sits are my best reading, not a survey. Part 1 of 4 The site What is there, and why it is hot 01 The site A building on the sidewalk, a parking lot behind it Topanga Willows fills the east side of Topanga Canyon Boulevard for one block, from Providencia Street down to Dumetz Road. The building is one long single-story bar, roughly 210 feet by 50, set right on the sidewalk with red awnings on both faces. [31] The owner lists it at 9,809 square feet. [1] The map shows a nail salon, a cleaner, a quilt shop, The Yoga Center and a pizza place; the owner also lists Starbucks and Yogis Grill. [1] [31] All the parking is behind the building, on the east: four rows of angled stalls on two one-way aisles, about 68 stalls, with driveways on Providencia and on Dumetz. Houses back onto the east edge. The whole lot has one small tree in it. [31] The owner counts about 30,463 vehicles a day on Topanga Canyon and 11,457 on Dumetz, with 114,413 people living within three miles. [1] A second listing gives 36,641 and 9,424, so I treat both as rough. [2] The orientation is the whole story. Because the building sits on the west side of its lot, it shades only the first row of stalls late in the day. The rest of the lot is in the sun from morning on. And the side people actually walk along, the storefronts on Topanga Canyon, faces west into the afternoon sun. One constraint: Topanga Canyon Boulevard is State Route 27, a Caltrans road. [29] The planted strip between the curb and the sidewalk is public right-of-way, so anything there is a request to the agencies, not something the owner can just build. Fig. 2: Existing conditions. Red hatching is paving in full sun. From aerial imagery Three photos this study still needs I worked from aerial and street imagery. These are the shots that would turn the estimates into evidence. Photo A Storefront sidewalk from the Dumetz corner, 3 pm, clear summer day What it would prove: That the west-facing walk is in full sun in the afternoon, which is the claim Fig. 1 rests on. Photo B The lot from the Providencia driveway at the same hour What it would prove: How far the building’s shadow really reaches, and that the other three rows get none (Fig. 2). Photo C The Dumetz corner and the one tree in the lot, with a person for scale What it would prove: Where people sit today and how small the existing canopy is, which sets the baseline for section 11. 02 The problem The hottest official reading in county history was taken a few miles from here Woodland Hills is one of the hottest parts of Los Angeles. A parking lot makes that worse in exactly the place people have to walk. 121°F Recorded at Pierce College in Woodland Hills on Sept. 6, 2020. It is the highest temperature at an official station in Los Angeles County. The old record, 119°F in 2006, was also Woodland Hills. [3] [4] 120–150°F Peak summer surface temperature of conventional paving, according to the EPA. [5] 1,500+ Extra emergency room visits in Los Angeles County on a hot day, from UCLA data reported by NBC Los Angeles. [9] NASA researchers found that heatwaves in Southern California got more frequent, more intense and longer from 1950 to 2020, with the biggest change in inland urban areas, which sit far from sea breezes and are covered in surfaces that store heat. [4] Tree canopy covers about 25 percent of the City of Los Angeles, and it is spread unevenly. [8] I do not have a canopy number for this block. Distance to Pierce College is my estimate; check it on a map. Part 2 of 4 The evidence What has been measured elsewhere 03 The evidence What the research says works I looked for measured results, not claims. Six findings shaped the design. Shade is the strongest tool. Shaded surfaces can be far cooler than the same material in the sun. [6] 20 to 45°F cooler at peak Trees also cool the air by releasing water through their leaves. [6] 2 to 9°F lower peak summer temperatures In a shopping center lot in Davis, California, the shaded half had cooler air, and cars parked there had cooler fuel tanks. [11] Air 1 to 2°C cooler; fuel tanks 2 to 4°C cooler Urban trees catch rain before it reaches the pavement. [7] 15 to 27 percent of annual rainfall absorbed Permeable paving has strong evidence behind it for cutting runoff and pollutants. [23] Rated “strong evidence” A Los Angeles study modeled more tree cover and more reflective surfaces and found fewer heat-related emergency room visits. [10] Peer reviewed, 2024 The catch: planting a tree is not the same as getting shade Sacramento has required 50 percent shade ove
